newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia to impose heavier penalties for corruption.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia to impose heavier penalties for corruption.

text.p: Malaysians found guilty of corruption will face heavier penalties under a new law, officials said, as the rapidly growing country steps up its anti-graft campaign.
The proposed Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Bill 1997 will be proposed in parliament next week, they said at a government conference on corruption at the weekend.
Under the bill, the maximum jail term will be increased to 20 years from seven years and the maximum fine raised to 100,000 ringgit ($38,000) from 10,000 ringgit ($3,800).
There had been suggestions earlier that whipping should also be imposed, but this was rejected by the cabinet.

Under the new law, a person facing corruption charges will be deemed to be guilty unless he or she can prove innocence. The accused will be required to prove that his or her wealth was legally acquired.
"The legal principle where one is innocent until proven guilty will not hold in corruption cases anymore," Education Minister Najib Razak told the conference.
A number of politicians are currently under investigation over allegations of corruption.
Last month, a federal deputy minister and two state politicians were sacked for alleged corruption.
In April, a senior Malaysian politician, who is facing trial for trying to take almost $1 million out of Australia, resigned as chief minister of central Selangor state.

He was detained at Brisbane International Airport on December 22 after the equivalent of US$940,000 in cash was found in his luggage and later charged with failing to declare an amount over A$5,000. He was also charged on a second count for making a false declaration.
Najib described corruption as a "non-military threat towards the very survival of the country."
"Its seriousness can be compared to threats from Communists, drugs and external threats."

"If corruption is institutionalised and made a way of life, it will inadvertently affect the country's political stability, ethics and economy. It will also make the rich, richer and the poor, poorer," he said.
The new law will also penalise those who falsely accuse another person of being corrupt.

Under the bill, those who are found to have made false allegations will be liable to a 100,000 ringgit fine or a 10-year jail sentence or both. This was aimed at protecting innocent people from being falsely accused, Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has said.
But some have labelled the new provision retrogressive, saying that it would dampen efforts to control and stamp out corrupt practices.

"While nobody would argue with Anwar on the need to protect innocent people from false allegations, especially in a matter as serious and shameful as corruption, we must also be mindful not to do things that may discourage the public from taking on a greater social responsibility," A. Kadir Jasin, group editor of the New Straits Times, said in his Sunday column.
